opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few places where they really shine, and it's worth separating them out because people sometimes lump them together.

The first is cost and latency at scale. If you have a well-defined task that you're running millions or billions of times — say, classifying documents, extracting fields from invoices, routing support tickets — you often don't need the full breadth of a frontier model. A much smaller model that's been tuned or distilled for that task can match the quality and be an order of magnitude cheaper and faster. In a lot of enterprise settings, that's the difference between something being economically viable or not.

The second is domain data that the general models just haven't seen. A lot of the most valuable data in the world is inside companies — their internal codebases, their schemas, their jargon, how they define a "customer" or "revenue." Frontier models are trained on the public internet, so they're great generalists, but they don't know that, at your company, a certain table is the source of truth and another one is deprecated. You can get a long way with retrieval and good context, but for some tasks, actually training on that data, or at least tuning on it, gives you a meaningful quality bump.

The third, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the real advantage usually isn't the model alone — it's the system. What we see over and over with customers is that the best results come from compound AI systems: a combination of models, retrieval, tools, and evaluation, all tuned together for a specific task. Within that, a specialized component — a reranker, a small model that checks SQL, a judge model trained on your own quality criteria — can make a big difference, even if the main reasoning step still uses a frontier model.

That said, I'd be careful about overclaiming. The frontier models keep getting better, and a lot of tasks that needed fine-tuning two years ago now just work with a good prompt and some examples. So my general advice is: start with the best general model, build good evaluations for your task, and then specialize where the evals tell you there's a gap — whether that's quality, cost, or latency. Specialization is a tool you reach for with evidence, not a default starting point.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that for most tasks today, if you just want the best quality on a one-off query, the frontier model is going to win. They're trained on everything, they generalize well, and they keep getting better. So the question is really, where does that stop being the right trade-off?

The first place is when you have a lot of volume on a narrow task. If you're running, say, a classification or extraction step over billions of documents, you don't need a model that can also write poetry and do competition math. You need something that does that one thing reliably and cheaply. We've seen a lot of cases at Databricks where a customer fine-tunes a much smaller model on the outputs of a frontier model, or on their own labeled data, and gets equal or better quality at a tenth or a hundredth of the cost and with much lower latency. And latency matters a lot once you're putting these into interactive products or into agent loops where you call the model many times.

The second place is domain-specific data that the general models just haven't seen much of. Every company has internal jargon, their own codebases, proprietary formats, telemetry, things that aren't on the public internet. A general model can be prompted around some of that, but if the task really depends on that private knowledge, specializing a model, whether through fine-tuning or through retrieval, tends to close the gap faster than waiting for the next frontier release.

The third thing I'd point to is control. When you own the model, you control the behavior, the version, the data governance, where it runs. A lot of enterprises care about that a great deal. You don't want your production system to change behavior because a vendor silently updated the model under you.

And then I think the thing people underestimate is that the real unit of value is not the model, it's the system. It's the retrieval, the tools, the evaluation loop, the data pipeline around the model. What we found with compound AI systems is that once you've built that scaffolding, swapping in a smaller specialized model for a particular component is often easy and very high leverage. So I don't see it as specialized versus general. I see it as, you use the general model to get started and to generate data, and then you specialize the pieces that are expensive or high-volume or sensitive. That's the pattern that keeps repeating.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest advantage is when you have a fairly well-defined task and you care about cost, latency, or consistency. A general frontier model has to be good at an enormous range of things. If your application is extracting information from documents or classifying support requests, you may be able to get the quality you need with a much smaller, specialized model.

The other opportunity is learning from feedback specific to your application. What counts as a good answer for your business might be quite different from what counts as a good answer in a general chat setting. If you can measure that and collect examples, you can optimize for it.

But I’d start with a strong general model to understand the task and establish a baseline. Specialization makes sense once you know where the general model falls short, or where running it is too expensive. And you can combine them: use a specialized model for the common cases and a more capable model for the difficult ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest advantage is when you have a well-defined task and some way to measure how well you’re doing. A general frontier model has to be good at a huge range of things, but an application might need to extract a few fields from documents or answer questions over a particular set of data. You can specialize for that workload and potentially get similar or better quality at much lower cost and latency.

The interesting part is that specialization doesn’t necessarily mean training a model from scratch. You can use a strong model to generate examples, then train a smaller model for the task, or build a system that routes the easy requests to a cheaper model and sends the harder ones to a frontier model. So I see a lot of opportunity at the level of the whole system: figuring out where you actually need the most capable model and where something much smaller is sufficient.
